category_title: Boys who have been victims of bullying and project parental advice into social interactions
minimal_context: The student is participating in a one-on-one role-play activity using a scarf to compare the feelings of a bully and a victim and offer advice.
dialogue:
TUTOR: For this part of our role-play, I am going to put on this scarf and pretend to be the victim. How do you think the victim is feeling right now?

STUDENT: His feelings are fear, loneliness, pain, sadness, hatred towards the bully and humiliation. He has no support from other children, so he cannot talk to anyone since nobody could really understand how he is feeling.

TUTOR: What about the bully? What could the bully do to solve the problem he created?

STUDENT: Apology would be the right thing to do in order to find a way out of his problem but at the same time it would be a mistake since by apologising he would show weakness and nobody would hold him in high esteem anymore.

TUTOR: Let's go back to the victim. What advice would you give to the victim to handle this situation?

STUDENT: He needs help. I would certainly become his friend. I would tell him to believe and trust himself. I would tell him to do whatever he likes and not to be afraid of other people... he has to believe that he can make it. Suppression of anger is the only way to deal with the problem, even though that is difficult without help from someone outside.

options.A: Change the entire structure of the one-on-one role-play sessions to keep the student's challenging behaviors down.
options.B: Meet individually to inform the student about the focus on difficult behavior, assure confidentiality, and give the option not to participate.
options.C: Implement a verbal communication book during the role-play sessions to help the student express feelings about the characters.
options.D: Radically remove time constraints for the role-play sessions, slowing down the pace of the activity as much as required.
